title: Single-Region vs Multi-Region
summary: One region is the right default until latency, availability, or data-residency law force you out of it — not because multi-region is impressive, but because each one multiplies your operational surface.

slides.markdown:
Most systems should run in **one region** until a specific, nameable force breaks that — not because multi-region is exotic, but because every extra region multiplies your replication, consistency, deployment, and on-call surface.

Think of a single region like a single office: fine for every customer and regulator until distance, an outage, or a law says otherwise. This topic gives you the three real forces that justify multi-region — **latency**, **availability**, **residency** — so you can tell a genuine trigger from a resume-driven one.

slides.sectionTitle: Why "one region" is the right default
slides.markdown:
A **region** is one geographic deployment — one set of data centers with its own compute, storage, and networking. Running in a single region means one database, one deployment pipeline, one consistency model, and no cross-region network hop to reason about.

A startup serving mostly US customers from `us-east-1` gets 99.9%+ availability, single-digit-millisecond internal latency, and a simple mental model, for a fraction of the engineering cost of running two regions. Multi-region adds real, ongoing tax: replication lag to manage, conflict resolution to design, twice the infrastructure to patch and monitor.

The interview move: start single-region, then name the specific force that would push you off it — don't reach for multi-region because it sounds more senior.

slides.sectionTitle: The three forces that push you multi-region
slides.markdown:
Three forces — and only three, in practice — justify the cost of multi-region. **Latency**: users far from your one region see slow responses that no amount of horizontal scaling inside that region fixes. **Availability**: a whole-region outage takes your service down completely, and some SLAs can't tolerate that blast radius. **Residency**: law or contract requires certain data to physically stay within a country or bloc.

Each force has a different fix — latency wants regions near users, availability wants a failover target, residency wants a boundary around specific data — so naming which one applies changes the design, not just the slide count.

The next few slides take latency and availability in turn; residency gets its own topic later in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a single-region system and its blast radius
slides.markdown:
![A single region containing the load balancer, app servers, and database inside a dashed blast-radius circle, with a region-wide outage taking down all traffic](assets/single-region-blast-radius.svg)

Everything inside one region shares fate: the load balancer, every app server, and the database all go dark together if that region's power, network, or control plane fails.

That's the trade you're accepting by staying single-region — total simplicity, but a blast radius that's the whole service, not a fraction of it.

slides.sectionTitle: Latency: physics sets a floor scaling can't fix
slides.markdown:
Light in fiber travels at roughly two-thirds the speed of light in vacuum, which puts a hard floor under round-trip time regardless of how much compute you throw at a region. New York to Singapore is about 15,000km one way — physics alone imposes something like 150ms round trip before your server does any work, and real networks add more.

Adding servers, caches, or bigger databases inside `us-east-1` does nothing for a user in Singapore: the request still has to cross the ocean twice. The only fix for distance-driven latency is a region physically closer to that user.

This is the tell that separates a latency problem from a capacity problem: if p99 latency is bad specifically for distant users while local users are fine, more horsepower in the existing region won't help.

slides.sectionTitle: Availability: what a full regional outage takes down
slides.markdown:
A regional outage isn't one server dying — it's the shared power, networking, or control-plane layer under an entire region failing, taking every app server and database replica inside it down together. Major cloud providers' single regions have had multi-hour outages a handful of times over the past decade — rare per region, but not zero, and the cost of one hitting you is total downtime, not degraded service.

A true multi-region setup survives this because a second region, with its own independent power and network, can take over. The cost is real: you now run and pay for infrastructure in two places, and need a way to fail traffic over (covered in the next topic).

The question to ask before paying that cost: what does an hour of full outage actually cost the business, and does that number justify a second region's steady-state bill?

"We have a backup region" and "we're multi-region" are different architectures with different guarantees.

| | Single-region + backup region | True multi-region |
|---|---|---|
| Who serves live traffic | Only the primary region | Two or more regions, concurrently |
| Steady-state cost | Backup mostly idle or cold | Full infrastructure cost in every active region |
| Failover | Manual or scripted cutover, minutes to hours | Traffic already flowing elsewhere, seconds |
| Complexity | Lower — one active system to reason about | Higher — replication, conflicts, routing across regions |

**How to decide:** if your RTO tolerance is minutes-to-hours and cost matters, a warm backup region is enough; if you need near-zero failover time or want to serve distant users from their nearest region day-to-day, you need true multi-region and its ongoing cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: going multi-region to solve a scaling problem
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We're running out of capacity in this region — let's go multi-region."

**Why it's wrong:** raw request or data volume within one region is almost always a horizontal-scaling problem — add app nodes, shard the database, add read replicas — not a geography problem. Multi-region adds cross-region replication, conflict handling, and routing complexity without addressing why the single region ran out of headroom.

**Correct model:** reach for multi-region only when the force is genuinely latency, availability, or residency — not capacity. A region that's saturated needs more capacity inside it first; going multi-region on top of an under-scaled single region just gives you two regions that are each still under-scaled.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: does multi-region actually pay for itself here?
slides.markdown:
Turn the availability trade-off into arithmetic instead of a gut call. Say a second active region costs an extra **$40,000/month** in duplicated infrastructure. Say the service generates **$5M/month** in revenue, and history suggests roughly **one 3-hour full-region outage per year** without a second region.

Three hours of downtime a year is about 0.03% of the year — against $5M/month (~$60M/year), that's roughly **$20,000** in lost revenue from the outage, versus **$480,000/year** ($40k x 12) to prevent it. On these numbers, a second region costs more than the outage it prevents — the honest conclusion is that a cheaper mitigation (a warm backup with a scripted failover, not full active-active) is the better trade, unless the outage also carries reputational or contractual costs the revenue number doesn't capture.

The senior-level habit isn't "always be resilient" — it's running this exact calculation before recommending the more expensive architecture, and being willing to recommend *against* multi-region when the numbers say so.
